canberra.title: Serial sex abuser found guilty of assaulting 11 people, including underage family members
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual abuse. A 46-year-old man has been found guilty of 32 sexual or indecent offences against 1...
canberra.content:
25 September 2026

Tyson Bonfield (centre, unblurred) approaches the ACT Courts for his trial. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual abuse.

A 46-year-old man has been found guilty of 32 sexual or indecent offences against 10 victims.

Tyson ‘Ty’ Bonfield pleaded not guilty to 43 charges related to 11 complainants in his ACT Supreme Court jury trial.

It had been alleged the abuse took place between the late 2000s and early 2020s against four female members of his own family when they were still children or teenagers, as well as against seven family friends – being three teenage girls, three women and one man.

The alleged abuse was not reported until one of the family members went to her mother in December 2020.

When police spoke to Bonfield in January 2024, he told them he hadn’t done anything wrong and described the initial claims against him as “bullshit”.

When the family members were cross-examined during his trial, barrister James Sabharwal suggested they made up the sexual assault allegations together. They denied this.

The trial ran for about three weeks before the jury began deliberating on Monday morning (21 September).

The jury returned guilty verdicts on 32 offences relating to all 11 victims on Friday (25 September).

Some of Bonfield’s supporters shook their heads at the jury box as the verdicts were read out.

Two not guilty verdicts were also recorded.

ACT Supreme Court Chief Justice Lucy McCallum thanked the jury for their service.

“This has been a hard trial,” she said.

“I hope that you have found some satisfaction in discharging your civic duty.”

The jury was discharged on the remaining nine counts.

The four family members named in the charges have provided their consent for the media to name Bonfield in reporting. While they were children or teenagers at the time of the alleged offending, they are now all adults.

As Bonfield has been found guilty of sexual or indecent offences against 11 people, he would have to be considered one of the most prolific sex offenders in the ACT.

His matter will return to court at a later date.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

You can also submit an online report about an historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Killer jailed for ‘excessive self-defence’ stabbing of father-of-four at rural property
canberra.snippet: Robert Mathew Marshall will spend at least the next three years and three months behind bars for killing 38-year-old Adam Cordingley in a...
canberra.content:
25 September 2026

Start the conversation

Robert Mathew Marshall was sentenced for manslaughter by the NSW Supreme Court. Photo: Julia Gomina.

Robert Mathew Marshall will spend at least the next three years and three months behind bars for killing 38-year-old Adam Cordingley in a case of “excessive self-defence”.

The now 43-year-old was originally charged with murder over the 23 March 2024 stabbing death but a jury found him guilty of manslaughter.

The court previously heard Mr Cordingley had been devastated when he learned his wife had a 12-month affair with Marshall that ended in mid-2023.

On the night of 23 March 2024, Marshall left the Terminus Hotel in Marulan (where he worked as a chef) and returned to his farm on Oallen Ford Road in Bungonia.

There he found Mr Cordingley on his property, wanting to speak about the affair.

A scuffle broke out between the two, during which Marshall used a hunting knife to stab Mr Cordingley three times. Two of those wounds proved fatal.

At the end of the trial, jurors rejected the then-42-year-old’s claims of self-defence when finding him guilty of a charge of manslaughter.

During his sentencing remarks, Justice Paul McGuire accepted it had been Mr Cordingley who was the “initial aggressor” that fateful night, as he was “fixated” on finding out the details behind the affair.

Marshall had pulled the hunting knife from its sheath during their conversation.

He told Mr Cordingley to leave several times, and when Marshall turned to walk away Mr Cordingley tore his t-shirt and punched him in the head.

Mr Cordingley said “did you stab me?” before Marshall ran off down the driveway and called Triple Zero.

“I find the offender became annoyed that the deceased was on his property and questioning him about the affair,” Justice McGuire said.

“His annoyance quickly escalated to anger and aggression … [the stabbings] were deliberate acts on the behalf of the offender.”

Justice McGuire accepted that Marshall hadn’t intended to harm or kill Mr Cordingley, but the fact he had armed himself and stabbed his victim three times showed his actions were “dangerous to a significant degree”.

“The acts of stabbing were deliberate … they were a spontaneous reaction to being punched,” he said.

“[However] the conduct was not a reasonable response to the circumstances.”

Justice McGuire said Marshall should have realised that by having the knife in the first place, he was exposing Mr Cordingley to a “serious risk” of injury.

He found Marshall’s offending was towards the lower end of the range of objective seriousness, that the offending hadn’t been planned, he had no prior criminal record, and that Marshall was a man of “prior good character”.

Justice McGuire was also satisfied Marshall was unlikely to reoffend in the future and his prospects of rehabilitation were good.

The court previously heard Mr Cordingley’s death had devastated his wife and four children.

It also heard Marshall expressed empathy for Mr Cordingley’s children and was genuinely remorseful for his actions.

“He expressed sadness and shock when he was told [Adam Cordingley] had died,” Justice McGuire said.

Justice McGuire sentenced Marshall to a total of six years imprisonment, backdated to begin on 27 April to take into account the 151 days he’s already spent in custody.

Marshall was handed a non-parole period of three years and eight months (also backdated), meaning he’ll be eligible to apply for release from 26 December 2029.

canberra.title: Perfect storm blows away 62-year-old timber truss and frame operation but business still intact
canberra.snippet: A Canberra company has shuttered its 62-year-old timber truss and frame manufacturing unit due to a perfect storm of market, economic and...
canberra.content:
CRT Building Products in Mitchell is a Canberra success story and still very much in business. Photo: Facebook.

A Canberra company has shuttered its 62-year-old timber truss and frame manufacturing unit due to a perfect storm of market, economic and cost pressures.

CRT Building Products this week announced it would no longer produce timber trusses and frames at its Mitchell factory for Canberra home builders, sparking fears, fuelled by a misleading social media post from Opposition Leader Mark Parton, that the business itself was closing.

The “structured exit” would mean the loss of 20 jobs, but general manager Richard Gianatti stressed that this was only one part of the business, which still employed more than 30 people, had a long history and still had a long future ahead of it.

“It was a decision not taken lightly because we’ve been in that industry since 1964,” Mr Gianatti said.

“It’s a commercial decision we made so as not to put the business into distress because we just didn’t see that [side of the business] was going to be profitable.”

A combination of the ongoing high cost of timber, competition from cheaper steel products, and a downturn in standalone home construction forced the company’s hand.

Mr Gianatti said the industry has never recovered from the 2019 bushfires, which wiped out pine plantations and sent timber costs through the roof.

The post-COVID construction boom that peaked in 2022 generated sufficient demand to absorb that higher cost, but since then rising inflation and interest rate rises have eroded housing affordability and dampened demand for new detached homes.

At the same time, the ACT Government wound back land releases for standalone housing and the market favoured high-rise residential towers that, of course, had no use for timber trusses or frames.

Mr Gianatti said the government was trying to keep land prices at the peak, but people couldn’t afford it.

“You pay $700,000 or whatever for a tiny block, you’ve got to at least spend that building on it, and people say ‘I can’t get the money, I don’t see the value’,” he said.

Mr Gianatti said standalone housing and townhouses were the company’s bread and butter, and while the former had slowed, the latter had dropped off significantly.

The Federal Government’s tax changes in the last budget also hadn’t helped.

“It might be well-intentioned, but possibly timed pretty poorly on the back of everything else,” Mr Gianatti said.

As if that wasn’t enough, the switch to cheaper steel along with cut-rate supply and install packages meant timber could not compete.

Canberra used to be a 95 per cent timber frame and truss market, but two large steel players now operated in the Territory that didn’t exist in 2019.

Mr Gianatti said the business was unlikely to restart the timber frame and truss operation even if conditions improved.

It needed to sell the equipment and repurpose the large shed housing it.

But CRT Building Products was still a substantial business and had plans to expand, Mr Gianatti said.

It had its own steel operation, Steeline Canberra, and was probably the biggest manufacturer of Colorbond roofing, guttering and fencing products in Canberra, as well as sheds. It also dealt in other products such as insulation.

“We’re a Canberra success story,” Mr Gianatti said. “The other side of the business is strong and will continue.”

CRT’s decision comes as confidence across the ACT property industry fell to the lowest level in Australia, with new survey results highlighting growing concerns about future investment, project activity and economic conditions.

The latest Procore/Property Council Confidence Survey shows the ACT’s confidence index has fallen to 55.6, well below the neutral benchmark of 100 and the lowest result recorded by any Australian jurisdiction.

Property Council ACT & Capital Region Executive Director Ashlee Berry said the results were a wake-up call for policymakers about the importance of maintaining a competitive and investment-friendly environment.

“The property sector wants to invest in Canberra, build the homes our growing city needs and create jobs, but this survey shows confidence has been significantly shaken,” Ms Berry said.

Ms Berry said the findings reflect growing concern about the cumulative impact of costs, regulation and uncertainty on development feasibility.

canberra.title: $140k fine after child’s hands catch fire at Questacon
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s popular science museum Questacon knew about the risk caused by the combination of plasma globes and hand sanitiser for m...
canberra.content:
The Department of Industry, Science and Resources was charged after a nine-year-old girl was burnt at Questacon. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Canberra’s popular science museum Questacon knew about the risk caused by the combination of plasma globes and hand sanitiser for months before a child’s hands caught fire at the facility.

On Thursday (24 September), the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR) was convicted and fined $145,000 over the incident that left the nine-year-old girl with serious burns.

In CCTV footage shown to the ACT Magistrates Court last month, viewers could see a packed gallery at Questacon filled with kids, adults and prams on 23 July 2022.

The nine-year-old was seen approaching a plasma globe and placing her hands on it. But she pulled her hands off straight away because they were covered in flames.

Her mother and a bystander put out the flames before she was taken to hospital.

Shortly before touching the globe, the girl had used the nearby alcohol-based hand sanitiser, provided by Questacon, and put five pumps of the substance onto her hands.

Magistrate Ian Temby, when sentencing the department on Thursday, said the girl was left with second degree burns to her hands, wrists and finger.

The department had pleaded guilty to a charge under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011, admitting it exposed visitors to a risk of death or serious injury.

Magistrate Temby said alcohol-based hand sanitiser was flammable. He said Questacon was aware there was a risk of fire from touching the plasma globes after using such hand sanitiser since February 2022.

That month, the museum had conducted a test and found a spark could be generated from the globes while using alcohol-based hand sanitiser.

Magistrate Temby said on one hand, the likelihood of the risk of fire eventuating was low. But on the other, the risk was foreseeable and had been identified in several risk assessments.

“Questacon’s response to the specified risk was inadequate. It failed to establish and maintain adequate safety protocols,” he said.

“[A] large number of people were exposed to the specified risk, including vulnerable members of the community such as children.”

Magistrate Temby said Questacon had no prior history of work health and safety offences, had a strong commitment to safety and was remorseful.

“I accept that Questacon provides a significant and valuable service to the community and to education,” he said.

“There is a low risk of the Commonwealth reoffending with respect to DISR’s operation of Questacon.”

A spokesperson for Comcare, which is the national authority for work health and safety, said DISR admitted it should have taken reasonably practicable measures to eliminate or minimise the risks by:

  • Arranging the plasma globe display so it could only have been subject to supervised use by trained Questacon workers
  • Replacing the alcohol-based sanitiser in the sanitiser stations with non-alcohol-based hand sanitiser or providing portable soap and water handwashing stations
  • Warning members of the public against using flammable substances, including alcohol-based hand sanitiser, before or when touching the plasma globes.

Comcare CEO Colin Radford said this was not an isolated event.

“The child’s injuries marked the sixth safety incident in five months involving the globes,” he said.

“This included a near miss in February 2022 where a staff member noticed the combination of hand sanitiser with metal could cause sparks from a plasma globe, and another incident that month where a visitor received a shock to a hand.

“Questacon’s response to these incidents was inadequate. It’s a large, interactive facility with inherent workplace health and safety risks that require a proactive approach and constant vigilance.”

Questacon is a division of DISR. In a statement, the department said it deeply regretted the incident.

“We acknowledge the impact and sincerely apologise to the young victim and their family,” the department said.

“We understand this was a distressing incident for them, and for other visitors and staff present on the day.

“Following the incident, Questacon took immediate action to close and then remove the exhibit and then undertook reviews.”

canberra.title: Andrew Antoniou’s vision of gardens introduced to Canberra’s Floriade at the Grainger Gallery
canberra.snippet: The idea of a garden traditionally implied an enclosed or protected piece of land – something that was safe and separated from the wilder...
canberra.content:
Andrew Antoniou, A girl’s own garden, oil on canvas, 110 x 153 cm. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

The idea of a garden traditionally implied an enclosed or protected piece of land – something that was safe and separated from the wilderness. Plants came a bit later, as did our modern idea of a horticultural enclosure, whether it be the backyard veggie plot, the botanical gardens or Floriade.

Andrew Antoniou is a London-born, Sydney-based artist who once taught at the Canberra School of Art and has exhibited in Canberra on numerous occasions.

Last year, he was diagnosed with cancer. Although he is now clear of cancer, the health scare had an impact on his life and art, and he has embraced in his work the theme of gardens, as a place of refuge, where hope and beauty are celebrated.

In his artist’s statement, Antoniou quotes a classic bestseller from the late last century, The Re-Enchantment of Everyday Life (1997), by former monk and psychotherapist Thomas Moore.

Moore writes, “The many great gardens of the world, of literature and poetry, of painting and music, of religion and architecture, all make the point as clear as possible: The soul cannot thrive in the absence of a garden.”

The gardens of Antoniou’s art are places of magical enchantment, where memories and daydreams combine, and nature and human endeavour collaborate to create something that should outlive the present and create something for posterity.

Andrew Antoniou, Gardener’s fortune, oil on canvas, 60 x 48 cm. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

The gardener, as found in the self-referential painting Gardener’s fortune, is a slightly naïve juggler who comes to bring enchantment to the garden.

A friend of mine once described gardening as an experiment in optimism. As Thomas Moore once argued, wonder and imagination are not childish qualities to be outgrown, but vital tools for coping with a world where alienation has become a norm.

Many figures in Antoniou’s works appear almost dreamlike, awkward in their movements and deliberate in their emotional intent. The artist treats his compositional spaces like stage sets, presenting elements for their symbolic and formal value.

Andrew Antoniou, North London Garden, oil on canvas, 51 x 40 cm. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

There are many memory paintings, including his North London Garden, which offers a glimpse of a walled garden set against a factory backdrop, bringing to mind William Blake’s “dark Satanic Mills”.

The garden is a small green oasis with tiny pegged-out vegetable plots.

The exhibition is dominated by two major oil paintings, Inside the Gates of Eden and A girl’s own garden, each over a metre and a half long.

The first revisits the Biblical Garden of Eden before the Fall with angelic gardeners busily at work looking after the botanical marvels. It appears to be set before Adam and Eve and the serpent arrived to spoil the party.

Andrew Antoniou, Inside the Gates of Eden, oil on canvas, 110 x 153 cm. Photo: Grainger Gallery.

In A girl’s own garden, three women plus a couple of wondrous birds cultivate the garden and celebrate the abundance of produce.

They are heavily drawn figures in brilliant garments who appear to be disproportionately large for their setting. The autobiographical context is not shared with the viewer, other than the idea that the garden is “a powerful metaphor where growth speaks of that beyond the material world”.

“Divination and ritual have always been deeply embedded in gardening practice to evoke the beings of the other world responsible for good harvest, divine beauty and spaces where these influences can come together with the everyday.”

Although Antoniou’s A Place Beyond may not be one of this artist’s most technically accomplished exhibitions, and I miss his monumental monochrome drawings for which he has national recognition, this celebration of the garden’s fecundity, beauty and magic has a quiet majesty.

Andrew Antoniou’s A Place Beyond is open at Grainger Gallery, 1/34 Geelong St, Fyshwick. It closes on 4 October. It’s open Thursday to Sunday, 11 am to 4 pm.

David Pocock calls for AI safety act after agent breach

The independent senator David Pocock says the recent AI agent breach raises serious questions about Australia’s approach to artificial intelligence regulation.

Speaking on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Pocock said the incident demonstrated the need for the government to introduce an AI safety act.

This is not a new problem. For many years now experts have been saying we need action on this. The crossbench has been pushing them. The government then said, ‘we’ll have some guardrails, we’ll put them on a website’ … that’s not enough. Clearly it’s not. This is a huge challenge facing us.

Qld parliamentary review of liability bill chooses not to hear from sexual abuse victims

A Queensland parliamentary committee reviewing a bill to overturn a ban on lawsuits by child sexual abuse victims against some employers has chosen not to hear from any victim-survivors.

The state Labor MP Meaghan Scanlon tabled the bill last year. It reverses a 2024 high court judgment ruling that the Catholic church was not legally responsible for the actions of a priest, because they were not a direct employee. The judgment also applies to all other employers.

Similar legislation has already passed parliaments in Victoria and the ACT.

The Queensland parliament’s justice, integrity and community safety committee held a single two-hour hearing into the bill this morning. The committee, which has a government chair, chose only to hear from lawyers.

Child abuse survivor Diane Carpenter said she was “devastated” not to be allowed to be heard by the inquiry and called for the bill to be passed.

If the bill is not passed, many adults who, as children, were abused in institutional care, will have no pathway to justice. Currently, we have two classes of victims: those who can access justice and those who can’t.

Retrial date for UK rapper accused of raping Australian fan

A new trial date has been set for a British musician and media personality accused of violently raping a fan in a hotel, after a jury was unable to reach a verdict, AAP reports.

Rapper Yung Filly, who is legally known as Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, faced trial in July over his 2024 encounter with a 20-year-old woman after a Perth nightclub gig.

The 31-year-old was found guilty of two assault offences and acquitted of three sexual penetration charges following an eight-day trial in Western Australia’s district court in July.

The jury was hung on three other sexual penetration counts and Barrientos is set to be retried for the charges.

He was not required to appear when the case returned to court on Friday and a fresh trial was listed for 2027.

The trial, beginning on 15 June in the same court, is expected to run for eight days.

Judge Linda Black previously permitted Barrientos to vary his bail so he could travel home to the UK while he awaits retrial. He is understood to have departed Perth in late August.

Who is James Ashby? Pauline Hanson’s ‘favourite son’

One Nation’s national director James Ashby wields as much – if not more – power over the party as Pauline Hanson herself.

Rafqa Touma speaks to Guardian Australia senior correspondent Sarah Martin about Ashby’s rise from PR flack to Hanson’s “favourite son” as One Nation’s popularity soars.

Australian shares on track for fourth straight losing week

The Australian share market has fallen to a three-month low and is headed for its fourth straight week of losses, as oil prices and bond yields both moved higher, AAP reports.

Near noon on Friday, the benchmark S&P/ASX200 index had fallen 0.43% to 8,664, its lowest level since mid-June, while the broader All Ordinaries had dropped 0.55%, to 8,848.2.

With a few hours of trading left, the ASX200 was on pace to finish the week down 0.8%, and was also 0.6% lower since the start of the year.

The Australian dollar was changing hands for 70.12 US cents, from 70.35 US cents at 5pm on Thursday.

Albanese said AI breach information was released as soon as possible

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says it’s “nonsense” to suggest the government may have released details about the OpenAI breach when it did because it suited him politically.

He told Sky News earlier:

It’s just nonsense. We were informed of this late. That’s one of the issues that I raised with Sam Altman when I spoke with him yesterday. I was informed while I’ve been in New York.

When pressed if the details were released as soon as possible, the prime minister said: “Absolutely”.

This was a unique situation. … We had to ascertain the facts, and then we made the statements, as a matter of urgency.

Albanese said he briefed the opposition as appropriate, and said Angus Taylor’s criticism was uncalled for.

He needs to act more like a responsible leader of an alternative government if he’s going to be taken seriously.

This is a unique situation without precedence.

More Queensland social housing dwellings vacant for longer

More social housing dwellings in Queensland are sitting vacant for longer, according to new data released by the state government.

The average downtime for a social housing dwelling has increased from 25.1 days last June to 42.7 days in July. Vacancy rates are slightly up from about 0.56% to 0.6%.

The data was released yesterday in response to a parliamentary question.

The number of people in the state’s emergency homelessness assistance scheme – which pays hotels and motels to accommodate them – has declined from 3,623 to 2,707. The state made many homeless people ineligible for the system last year.

There has been a slight increase in the number of Queenslanders in the state’s public housing system, from 55,913 to 55,998, but a decline in the number on the social housing waiting list, from 53,874 last September to 46,037 in July.

Sarah Martin

One Nation admits using party funds to build $56,000 shed on James Ashby’s private property

One Nation has admitted using party funds to build a $56,000 shed on James Ashby’s private property.

Guardian Australia revealed on Monday that a company linked to One Nation – Small Batch Brewing Pty Ltd – was the purchaser of the shed on Ashby’s property despite having no revenue stream and not being licensed to make or sell alcohol.

Ashby is living in the shed on his Yeppoon property while he undertakes renovations.

In an email sent to members on Thursday night, the party’s general manager, Kelvin Morton, said party funds had been used to build the shed.

australia.title: PM rejects ‘nonsense’ suggestion he delayed revealing OpenAI Medicare hack as Labor considers changing laws
australia.snippet: Expert says Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a ...
australia.content:
The federal government could change Australian laws if the current legal framework could not respond to the unprecedented OpenAI hack of Medicare, ministers have confirmed.

It comes as the prime minister denied accusations from the opposition he had held on to the information before announcing it at the UN general assembly in New York, and said it was released at the first possible opportunity.

“It’s just nonsense … I was informed while I’ve been in New York,” Anthony Albanese told News24 on Friday.

“Imagine if we had said there’s been a data breach, but we don’t know what has been sourced, we don’t know if your personal information is out there, that would have created a great deal of anxiety, which was unnecessary.

“We had to ascertain the facts, and then we made the statements, as a matter of urgency, we also provided briefings to the opposition, as is appropriate.”

The government services minister, Katy Gallagher, said she was informed about the breach on 17 September. Guardian Australia understands she informed the prime minister between Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September.

Albanese left for the US on the Friday, where he first met Apple’s executive chair, Tim Cook, in California on Saturday morning, before flying to New York that afternoon.

On Friday, the government said the review by spy agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, would consider whether legislative change was needed after Albanese revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare’s statistics website and three other systems in June.

If current laws could not touch the tech company, they would need updating, environment minister, Murray, Watt said on Friday.

“There’s now a review of this under way through that taskforce that we’ve appointed, and one of the things that they’ll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian federal police under current Australian law,” he told Channel Seven’s Sunrise program.

“If that is possible to happen, then that will happen. If it’s not possible, then clearly that indicates that we need to change Australian laws, and that’s what we’ll be doing.”

The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, acknowledged similar incidents would become “more and more prevalent into the future” and the government would need to be prepared.

“That’s why we’re conducting a review of the incident as well as a review of the laws to determine exactly … whether there needs to be legislative change to recognise this type of incident conducted by an AI agent rather than directly by a person or a company,” Charlton told ABC radio.

Albanese told the Asia Society on Thursday that the incident was a “wake-up call” about the risks of AI, and whether humans would remain in charge of the technology.

“This technology is moving very, very fast, and we need to make sure that we have a responsibility to keep on top of it,” Albanese said.

Labor has announced it would legislate an AI standard, which Charlton said would be informed by the rapid review. The government has said it wants the bill to be introduced by the end of the year.

UNSW professor Lyria Bennett Moses, an academic expert in technology and law, said Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault, such as intention or knowledge, is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime.

She said existing laws are clear if a human or corporation gains unauthorised access to restricted data, but it’s more complicated when an AI agent commits the physical element of the offence.

“The person is not the AI agent, so it’s not about what the AI agent intended. It’s about how you attribute that intention and that knowledge back to a corporation,” Bennett Moses said.

Bennett Moses said existing civil laws are more likely to deal with these sorts of incidents, that would allow a government or individual to seek compensation an AI company for harm “negligently caused by that corporation”.

“If their systems have suffered harm and there is financial loss, and that harm was caused by the negligence of a corporation, you’ve got a potential for litigation to get compensation for that harm,” she said.

“Here it seems to me much easier to hold a company liable, because if a company caused the harm, it’s not a defence to say that my bot did it.”

Independent senator, David Pocock said the incident “raises serious questions” for the government after it initially, in 2024, considered mandatory guidelines for high-risk AI but then dropped them in late 2025.

“It’s great to see the PM on the world stage saying that we need global cooperation on this. We absolutely do. This is a huge challenge facing us. But it’s a bit rich where at home you’ve shelved plans for an AI safety act.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told reporters the Coalition would be open to working with the government to hold companies accountable.

“I’ve long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it … But we’ll wait and see what the government has in mind.”

OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, said on Thursday the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.

Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

australia.title: The rise of Dom Dolla: what the DJ’s record-breaking stadium show for 60,000 fans tells us about music today
australia.snippet: Dom Dolla’s enormous show in Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium set a new record for a solo EDM artist in Australia, and proves how the genre is ...
australia.content:
“Abandon all hope, ye who enter,” it says on the wall – no, my mistake, that is just the sign for the Johnnie Walker bar at Marvel Stadium. I have a theory that what everyone is drinking at a show can tell you a lot about the mood of a crowd, and based on the stacks of Hard Solo and Walker cans strewn on the streets outside Dom Dolla’s biggest ever show, 60,000 people are in for an intense, sticky night.

And a significant one. That 60,000 people have turned out to see a DJ play in a stadium, the biggest electronic dance music (EDM) concert by a solo artist ever staged in Australia’s history, tells us something about the way music is changing – both in Australia and outside it.

Australia currently ranks as the world’s third-largest streaming market for EDM (behind the US and Germany). Australian EDM is our most popular genre internationally on Spotify. And Dom Dolla – real name: Dominic Matheson – is part of the current charge, along with the likes of Rüfüs Du Sol, Flume, Fisher, Cyril, Alison Wonderland, Confidence Man, Pnau and The Avalanches. Some of these names may seem old, but the heights of their successes are new.

Dom Dolla’s 2024 national tour was the largest-ever staged by an Australian electronic artist: 170,000 tickets sold. He sold out Madison Square Garden – twice – in 2025. After Thursday’s record show in Australia, he will set another record in New Zealand in February when he puts on the biggest-ever electronic music event in the country’s history.

Dom Dolla has not achieved this success by reinventing the wheel. He has hit a sweet spot between the EDM purists, the tech house fans and the mainstream. There are no surprises; the bass drops exactly when you think it will. He remixes Kings of Leon, Billie Eilish and Technotronic. It is reliable, it is fun.

Some of his appeal also has to do with his particularly understated Australian charm. He doesn’t muck about with small talk, other than to share his wonder at his own spectacle. “This is absolutely fucking mental, I love it,” he says, to wild cheers. A bit later: “This is absolutely fucking insane.” More cheers. When I ask around among the crowd why everyone loves him so, the consensus is: he’s a local boy done good.

Does EDM work in stadiums? Yes and no. Putting the roof on Marvel Stadium doesn’t make it cosy. An arena or stadium is never going to capture the cramped intensity of a club. But they do allow for ground-shaking sound and spectacle, and Dom Dolla has fire balls, fireworks and lasers out the wazoo. The crowd’s energy feels febrile, edgier than other stadium shows I’ve been to recently; a lot of women are dragging their drunk friends along with the grim intensity of a prison guard. This is now “the world’s biggest nightclub”, as Dom Dolla puts it – and it is messy.

With an hour to go, the bass suddenly disappears. There has been some kind of technical snafu, which Dom Dolla keeps smoothly playing through. But the mood in the crowd very noticeably shifts. He’s up there all by himself. They smell blood. When the bass comes back 20 minutes later, the scream of 60,000 elated people takes the roof off. All is well again.

I personally love EDM because it can bring on a euphoric meditative state. Alive 2007 by Daft Punk, their live recording from Paris, is my most played album for a reason: the crowd. I love the whoops and roars more than the clinical precision of any of their studio albums. And I think about the lives of everyone at that Paris gig – the bad days at work, the arguments in the car, the mundane frustrations – and how none of that would have mattered to everyone during that show. At Dom Dolla, my mind goes to strange places as we writhe and sweat. I think about how I should have bought shares in Hard Solo. I think about dopamine and how EDM taps into something in our caveman brains. I think about how dancing in a crowd makes us feel connected to complete strangers. And at some point I realise, blissfully, I am no longer thinking at all.

australia.title: NSW cop asked friend ‘what would you do if I told you I killed somebody’ before alleged murders, court told
australia.snippet: Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington terrace in early 2024 Follow our A...
australia.content:
Beau Lamarre-Condon asked a friend, “What would you do if I told you I killed somebody?” nine months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a Sydney court has heard.

The New South Wales police officer then assured the friend he hadn’t killed anyone, before admitting he had entered Baird’s house while he was away, before stealing a Polaroid camera and eating an Easter egg.

Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Baird, 26, and his partner, Davies, 29, with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

It’s alleged he hid the bodies in surfboard bags when removing them from the house and CCTV footage of Lamarre-Condon buying a bag was released by the court on Friday.

The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court on Friday that the policeman had become “infatuated” with Baird during their brief relationship.

When the relationship ended in April 2023, Cook said Lamarre-Condon continued to speak about Baird.

He asked her a concerning question when they went to dinner a month later, Cook told the jury.

“One of the first things he said was, ‘What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?’” she told the jury.

Cook told Lamarre-Condon she wouldn’t help as she didn’t want a ghost haunting her, the court was told.

Lamarre-Condon laughed it off and said: “Don’t worry I didn’t do that, but I did do something crazy.”

Cook told the court the policeman said he had been watching Baird from outside his home, including on one occasion when he had friends over.

Lamarre-Condon saw Baird and his friends take photos using a Polaroid camera the officer had given him as a gift, Cook said.

When the group left Baird’s home, Lamarre-Condon had seen where the house key had been placed, Cook said.

“He had got the key, unlocked the door, stole the Polaroid camera and ate Jesse’s Easter egg,” she said on Friday.

Lamarre-Condon would travel to Baird’s home in his mother’s car and wear a black hoodie so he wouldn’t be recognised, the court was told.

The policeman and Baird began seeing each other again briefly a few months later.

But Baird ended the relationship in November 2023 after the accused went through his phone and deleted messages from other men. Lamarre-Condon was “really upset”, according to another one of the officer’s friends, Shae Davison.

Lamarre-Condon asked to stay at her house because he did not want to be alone, Davison told the jury.

The police officer arrived at her home with a backpack the next day and asked to send a message from her Instagram to Baird as “one last try to win Jesse back”, she told the court.

But Lamarre-Condon did not want her to read the message, claiming there were medical details he did not want her to know.

She didn’t want to do it initially but said: “He put a lot of pressure on me, he said he never asked anything of me, he’s so upset, can I help.”

“He wore me down,” Davison said on Friday. “It felt like guilt-tripping to me and using my friendship to get what he wanted.”

She agreed, on the condition Lamarre-Condon read out the text to her, while leaving out the medical details.

When he read out the message, she asked him to delete parts that weren’t true, and it looked like he was typing and actioning her edits, she told the court.

He then sent the note in a series of messages, and told her she was allowed to read it after 4 December 2023, when he told her he was set to undergo surgery. He left her home about an hour after he arrived.

The 1,600-word Instagram note claimed Davison had gone to Westmead hospital with Lamarre-Condon.

“He was told he had a cancerous tumour growing in his left shoulder joint/ligament area,” the text read out in court stated.

“Worst-case scenario, it could result in … possibly having his arm amputated.

“He was then immediately subscribed [sic] numerous medications … everyone knows these medications are some of the strongest you can be subscribed, which throw off your hormones massively, which throws off how a person can act in their day to day life.”

The friend told the jury she had not attended the hospital with Lamarre-Condon, nor did he clear this part of the text with her.

The messages tried to justify the officer going through Baird’s phone and stated “this is very out of character for him”.

“There is real love there, trust can be built back on that,” the note purportedly from Davison stated. “Even if you guys never hang out again, I know Beau wants to make things right.”

The friend was unsure if Baird read the messages but said it was possible he had seen them through Instagram’s preview function. Lamarre-Condon later asked her to unsend the messages.

She obliged and tried to ask him about the content of the messages but he did not want to talk about them.

“He was quite annoyed, I could tell in his voice he was frustrated that I had [read them],” she said.

It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.

The defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

world.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
world.snippet: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government There are growing fears of a retu...
world.content:
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.

Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.

A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”

The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.

In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.

Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.

The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.

On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.

In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.

AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
world.snippet: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market Nils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s ...
world.content:
A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.

The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.

Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.

Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.

“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”

Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”

Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.

Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.

Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.

Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.

The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.

Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

world.title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
world.snippet: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality One of South Africa...
world.content:
One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.

Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.

Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.

South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.

Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.

The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.

Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.

Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.

“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”

When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.

Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.

Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

world.title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns
world.snippet: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID ...
world.content:
The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put healthcare in Africa and the global south “under growing strain” a new report warns.

The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.

The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.

A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.

The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.

External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.

The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.

Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.

At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m after the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.

The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.

“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”

Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.

“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”

The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. About 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of more than 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.

The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.

The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

world.title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals
world.snippet: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is o...
world.content:
Nika’s story

No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.

Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.

Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.

Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.

After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.

“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”

The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?

Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.

It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.

The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.

A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.

A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.


The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.

Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.

The rug pull

Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.

Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.

Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.

Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.

This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.

Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.

For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.

Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”

African deals

When Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.

A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going.”

Kuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.

She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.

In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.

“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”


The drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire to end most migration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.

Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its name incorporating a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.

Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.

They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.

The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.

Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.

On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.

“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.

During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”

Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.

The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”

He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”

Malaria

Onboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.

For several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.

Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.

US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.

When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”


Back in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.

The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.

The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”

As the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.

Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.

In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.

According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.


Nika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”

The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.

An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”

Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.

“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”
